createOrReplace.title: AI in Insurance: IRDAI Says 85% of Insurers Use AI
createOrReplace.html:
AI in insurance is now the norm in India: IRDAI chairman Ajay Seth said on 19 November 2026 that nearly 85% of insurers use AI in some form, including underwriting and claims, according to Business Standard. In the same speech he asked whether humans still take the final decision, and flagged model risk, data grabs before quotes and grievance handling as the regulator's concerns.

This matters because the regulator has moved from encouraging AI to asking who is accountable for it. Seth spoke at the 11th Gatekeepers of Governance summit in Mumbai, the Free Press Journal reports, and urged insurers to train models properly and keep humans in charge. For Indian insurers, TPAs, brokers and the hospitals that deal with them, the question is no longer whether to use AI in claims and underwriting. It is whether they can show a board, an auditor or an ombudsman how a model reached its decision.

TL;DR

  • IRDAI chairman Ajay Seth said nearly 85% of Indian insurers use AI in some form, citing an expert study led by IIIT Hyderabad's director.
  • Around 60% of grievances reconsidered by senior insurer executives are settled in the policyholder's favour, Seth said, which suggests the first decision was often wrong.
  • Gen Re's 2025 survey found 65% of 17 Indian life insurers do not use system automation to spot suspicious claims; only 17.6% use AI or ML detection.
  • Among 5 non-life insurers in Gen Re's survey, 80.0% use AI or ML claims detection and 100.0% expect fraud-tech budgets to rise.
  • India's insurance penetration was flat at 3.7% in FY25, so insurers need cheaper servicing and faster claims to grow.

What did IRDAI say about AI in insurance?

IRDAI chairman Ajay Seth said nearly 85% of insurers now use AI in some form, and warned that model risk and human oversight are the new problems the regulator is dealing with.

Business Standard reports that Seth attributed the 85% figure to a recent study by a group of experts headed by Sandeep Kumar Shukla, director of IIIT Hyderabad. He described AI as a source of innovation and efficiency, then asked the question boards should be answering: "Are humans in charge of taking the final decision?" Elets BFSI and MediaNama carried the same figure, and the Free Press Journal reported that Seth named underwriting and claims as the main areas of use.

Seth also criticised insurers that ask for personal data before showing a premium quote, and said IRDAI plans to set up two industry working groups within 10 days to improve transparency in health claims processing, according to Business Standard.

Why is IRDAI worried about AI in claims?

Because claims decisions are where customers get hurt, and the regulator's own grievance data suggests too many first decisions are reversed on review.

According to Business Standard, Seth said around 60% of grievances reconsidered by senior executives inside insurance companies end up resolved in favour of policyholders, and around 60% of the remaining cases taken up by insurance ombudsmen go the same way. If a model is trained on past decisions that were later overturned, it will repeat them faster. That is the model risk Seth is pointing at.

Volume makes the stakes concrete. IRDAI data reported by Devdiscourse shows 1,37,361 health insurance grievances in FY 2024-25, of which 93% were resolved within the year. The same data puts the health claims paid ratio, by number of claims, at 87.50% in 2024-25, up from 82.46% in 2023-24 and 85.66% in 2022-23. IRDAI's rules also require cashless pre-authorisation within one hour and final authorisation within three hours of a discharge request.

How far has AI in insurance actually gone in India?

Further in general insurance than in life insurance: Gen Re's 2025 surveys show non-life insurers use AI for claims detection far more often than life insurers do.

Gen Re's 2025 India life fraud survey covered 17 life insurers. It found 65% do not use system automation to identify suspicious claims. Only 17.6% use AI or ML detection platforms, while 83.3% rely on rules-based triggers. Just 23.5% auto-adjudicate any claims, and 29.4% use AI to spot questionable risks at underwriting. Budgets are moving, though: 70.6% expect fraud-prevention technology spend to rise.

The non-life survey is small, five companies, so read it as a direction rather than a market share. Of those, 80.0% use AI or ML claims detection, 60.0% auto-adjudicate some claims, 40.0% use AI at underwriting and 100.0% expect their fraud-tech budget to grow. The same 80.0% said suspicious claims have increased since COVID-19.

Where does AI pay off for insurers today?

In servicing and fraud triage first, where volumes are high and each decision is small, rather than in final claim rejections.

ICICI Lombard offers a recent example. In an interview reported by Elets BFSI on 22 November 2026, the insurer said its contact centre handles six to seven lakh queries a month. When digitisation started, about 20% of interactions were digital; now 71–75% are, more than 40 lakh interactions a year. A manual call costs about ₹50, so handling everything by people would cost about ₹20 crore a year, against no more than ₹3 crore for digital servicing. The company puts the cost avoided at ₹17 crore a year, an estimate rather than a reported saving.

Fraud triage is the second payoff. A Policybazaar report covered by The Tribune said AI flagged around 11% of term insurance cases and 16% of savings plan cases for possible fraud, and that chatbots handle over 30% of first-contact queries, up from 15% a year earlier. Those are vendor-reported figures; treat them as a sign of where AI is used, not as a benchmark.

Is fraud pressure on Indian insurers rising?

Yes. Digital onboarding has made identity fraud easier, and India's suspected digital fraud rate runs well above the global average.

TransUnion data reported by ET BFSI and Cafemutual found 7.1% of consumer digital transactions in India in 2025 were suspected fraud attempts, against a global average of 3.8%. Gen Re's non-life respondents named remote and digital customer interactions and difficulty obtaining evidence as top factors raising their fraud exposure. Gen Re's life survey found only 47% of respondents involve law enforcement and 29% share data with the Insurance Information Bureau.

Enforcement is also active. Elets BFSI notes IRDAI recently imposed a ₹2 crore penalty on Star Health. A model that rejects valid claims creates grievances; one that misses fraud creates losses. Insurers need both error rates measured.

What does AI in insurance mean for growth?

AI is one of the few levers insurers have to lower the cost of serving small policies, which matters because penetration has stalled.

Business Standard's summary of the IRDAI annual report shows insurance penetration flat at 3.7% in FY25. Life penetration slipped to 2.7% from 2.8% in FY24, and Angel One notes it was 3.2% in FY22. Non-life penetration stayed at 1%. Life premium income rose 6.73% to ₹8.86 lakh crore, and health premiums grew 9.19% to ₹1.18 lakh crore, making health more than 41% of non-life premiums. Health is also where claims volumes, hospital paperwork and grievances concentrate, so it is where AI in claims will be tested hardest.

How should insurers and TPAs put human oversight around AI?

Treat every model that touches a claim or a price as a decision system with an owner, a log and a human override, and report on it to the board.

  1. Inventory every model. List each AI or rules engine used in underwriting, claims, pricing and servicing, with a named business owner.
  2. Classify by harm. Separate models that only route or prioritise from those that approve, reject or price. The second group needs human sign-off on adverse decisions.
  3. Log the reasons. Store the inputs, model version, score and reason codes for every decision, so a grievance officer or ombudsman can see why.
  4. Measure reversals. Track how often grievance reviews overturn model-assisted decisions. With 60% of reviewed grievances going the customer's way, this is the metric IRDAI is watching.
  5. Collect only what you need. Do not ask for personal data before a quote unless pricing depends on it; Seth named this practice directly.
  6. Retrain on corrected outcomes. Feed overturned decisions back as labelled data so the model learns from reviews, not from its own mistakes.

What this means for Indian businesses

For insurers, the message from IRDAI is that adopting AI is not the achievement; governing it is. For TPAs, brokers and hospitals, expect more scrutiny of claims documents and faster turnaround demands, since cashless authorisation clocks are already one hour and three hours. For any BFSI firm building its own models, the cheapest time to add decision logs, reason codes and human override is before go-live, not after a grievance spike.

From the way we build AI systems at Fine Solves, the work that holds up under audit is usually unglamorous: clean claims data, explicit decision rules around the model, and an override screen that a claims manager actually uses. Frequently asked questions

What percentage of Indian insurers use AI?

Nearly 85% of Indian insurers use AI in some form, IRDAI chairman Ajay Seth said on 19 November 2026. Business Standard reports he cited a study by experts led by IIIT Hyderabad director Sandeep Kumar Shukla. The main uses are underwriting and claims, according to the Free Press Journal's report of the same speech.

Does IRDAI allow insurers to reject claims using AI?

IRDAI has not banned AI in claims, but its chairman has asked whether humans are in charge of the final decision. The safe approach is to let models triage, flag and prioritise, and keep a named person accountable for every rejection, with the reasons logged so grievance officers and ombudsmen can review them.

How are Indian insurers using AI for fraud detection?

Mostly through rules plus a growing layer of machine learning. Gen Re's 2025 survey found 83.3% of life insurers use rules-based triggers but only 17.6% use AI or ML detection, while 80.0% of the non-life insurers surveyed use AI or ML. Non-life insurers lead because motor and health claims arrive in higher volumes.

What is the health insurance claims paid ratio in India?

IRDAI data reported by Devdiscourse puts the health insurance claims paid ratio, by number of claims, at 87.50% in 2024-25, up from 82.46% in 2023-24. The same data shows 1,37,361 health insurance grievances in FY 2024-25, with 93% resolved within the year.

What should hospitals and TPAs expect from AI in insurance?

Faster, more automated document checks and tighter scrutiny of bills and pre-existing conditions, which Gen Re's non-life respondents ranked among the most common fraud types. Hospitals with clean, digital discharge summaries and itemised bills will clear cashless authorisation faster; those relying on scanned paper will see more queries.
